paragraphs: As to their citing the verse (Deut 1:5), "Moses undertook to expound this Torah," and saying that Moses "expounded it for them at ʿeber ha-Yarden" — we do not deny that. What we deny is the further claim that this "exposition" is the Mishnah and the Talmud. That is a claim without evidence; rather, their case for it is corrupt from several angles.

In the Mishnah and Talmud, the sages disagree extensively; they dispute with one another in many of their statements and the disputes among them are explicit on the page. If what is fixed in those works were naql (transmitted oral tradition), it would not be possible for each one of them to advance a different position and then to settle on one of the positions. The very fact of dispute, followed by settlement, shows that what is settled is settled by argument, not by recognition of transmission; for were it naql, the disputation would be otiose.

Naql is what is in the hands of the entire people, with no disagreement among them; rather, they are all of one mind on it, requiring no extraction or inference. Whenever some matter is in the hands of only a few, it is raʾy (opinion), not naql. Third angle: as we have already noted, the schools of Shām and ʿIrāq (Palestine and Babylonia) diverge on substantive matters; their divergences entail that each school excommunicates the other on the disputed points and excludes the other from the religion. The two cases together: either both schools' positions are naql — which is impossible, since the two positions contradict each other and Scripture itself says (Num 15:15), "one law shall be for the assembly"; some of them have an answer to this which we will mention and refute later — or only one school's position is naql. If only one — which one? Each side claims that it is the sound transmitter. This is the disagreement, the divergence, and within it lies the falsity of their naql-claim.

A fourth angle: their own dictum (cited in Baba Batra p. 12a): "the wise man is greater than the prophet." The principle behind the dictum is that the prophet only knows what is told to him by another (i.e., by the Creator, mighty and exalted), whereas the wise man extracts from himself. If, therefore, the "wise men" they invoke are these same Rabbanites — they are not in fact wise, since they only report what was told to them and learned by them. And if they are in fact wise, extracting from themselves — then what are they transmitting? This is again the bone in their throats. We have already noted that the very proponent of their argument negated what he had advanced when he said that the sages "pursue and infer one thing from another" — i.e., that they perform inference. Inference is qiyās, not naql.

A fifth angle: what they have made explicit in the Mishnah about sighting the new moon (reʾiyat ha-levanah) and their current reliance on the calendrical calculation (ʿibbur ha-shanah), and their claim that the calculation is ancient — given how this conflicts with naṣṣ, qiyās, and ijmāʿ all together. We will give a thorough treatment of this in our discussion of the new moons. Saadia used to say that the calculation goes back to Adam; later he came to say it goes back to Moses. This much is enough.[{2}]

A sixth angle: their dictum at Mishnah Shabbat 19:5: "the child is circumcised on the eighth day [from his birth], or on the ninth, or on the tenth, or on the eleventh, or on the twelfth." This entails that Rosh Hashanah can fall on a Sunday — which contradicts their current practice (which prevents Rosh Hashanah from ever falling on Sunday). We will give a full and clear discussion of this in the discussion of the new moons, and there we will also mention other statements of theirs that falsify their naql-claim.

A seventh angle: what we have already reported about statements of theirs that fall into kufr and ilḥād (unbelief and heresy) — such as the measurements of the [divine] stature[{3}] and others that are recorded in the Talmud, of which we have already mentioned some and of which there is much more we have not mentioned.

As to their citing the verse (Deut 17:8) — "if a matter is too hidden from thee in judgment" — no competent reasoner can argue from this for the Rabbanite case. The pericope is plain and explicit, not obscure or closed: "Thou shalt arise and go up …" (v. 8), "And come to the Levitical priests …" (v. 9). We have explained this in the preceding bab and shown that this very statement obligates qiyās, not the abandonment of it.[{4}] Even granted arguendo that the statement were generic and addressed to every wise man — including the lay wise — it still would not obligate what they claim. For the wise men of every age differ in their wisdom; the one of greater wisdom is more powerful at extraction than the one of lesser; and he infers from realities what the lesser cannot infer. This is against them, not for them. If the farāʾiḍ were all known by naql, with the naql in the hands of the whole community, how could any matter be hidden from the priests at the gates (the city-courts) and known only to the Great Priest in the Temple? Indeed, were he the only one to know even one such matter, the very naql claim is broken — for if even one matter falls outside the naql in the hands of the people, the claim that all the farāʾiḍ are known by naql is false. It is sufficient against them to cite (Deut 17:12): "And the man who acts presumptuously and refuses to hearken unto the priest …" — note that Scripture says "the priest" (singular, the great one), not "the priests" (plural). The verse therefore commands acceptance from the Chief Priest, who is just below the prophet, and the judge who stands in his place — not from a generic class of "wise men" of all sorts.

As to their claim that one must obey the wise and accept their statement — that is our claim too. The difference is this: what is obligatory upon us is to accept the statement of those wise men who adduce sound proof (al-burhān al-ṣaḥīḥ) for what they say — proof on which no impeachment lies. We are not obligated to accept and follow the statement of one who claims to be wise but whose statement contradicts Scripture.[{5}]

As to what they mentioned about the words we read differently from how they are written — and the rest of what they mentioned in this kind of argument — we do not derive these from "the Rabbanites' statement" or from the statement of any individuals. Rather, we have received them from the whole nation by naql — by both oral statement and by writing — exactly as we received the Torah from the whole nation. (And as to their statement that God "approved of the wise and made them greater than the prophets," etc. — this is recycled chatter, which we have already addressed; this passage in fact tells against the naql-claim they wish to establish from it.)

As to what they mentioned about passages that suggest contradiction — Deut 16:1 (Exodus by night) and the rest — and their claim that the ketuba and qiddushin details are unspecified in Scripture: the meanings of most of these matters can be extracted by qiyās and taʾwīl (interpretation). Some are recoverable by inferring from the beginning of a passage to its end, or from the end to the beginning, by various devices we will explain. In some of these matters the Rabbanites have themselves produced evidently corrupt claims, which themselves falsify the very naql they would derive from them. We will mention some examples in due course.

We further put this point to them: the Muslims ask us how we know that Moses' prophecy is sound. We reply that the muʿjizāt of Moses are transmitted by a vast community (jamāʿa kabīra) on whom collusion is excluded — i.e., the testimony rises to tawātur-level. They counter that the same can be said of their own prophet. The distinction we draw is this: our reports are written down in a book (the Torah) which the whole community received without dispute; everyone — small and great, female and male — knows it; the inscribed dīwān preserves it and excludes both addition and subtraction. By contrast, the muʿjizāt they claim for their prophet are not in a book; rather, the transmission is "X reported on the authority of Y" — a chain of personal authority that can be broken, augmented, or fabricated. The two are not comparable.

The same critique now binds the Rabbanites in their claim about the Oral Torah. By their own logic: an oral tradition that is not written down admits of addition and deletion; even most of it might be forgotten, especially under exilic-conditions of abandonment and persecution. This vitiates the Rabbanite naql-claim. If they reply, "but it is collected in the Mishnah and Talmud — those works are the codification of the Oral Torah" — we ask: why was it not codified in the era of the prophets, when the whole community could have transmitted it? In fact, the Mishnah was codified some two hundred years after the cessation of prophecy. Proof of this is their own statement at the head of the Mishnah (Avot 1:1): "Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and transmitted it to Joshua; Joshua to the Elders; the Elders to the Prophets; and the Prophets transmitted it to the Men of the Great Assembly." The Men of the Great Assembly, by the Rabbanites' own account, were those in the age of Zerubbabel, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. They then claim that Simeon the Just was one of the last of the Great Assembly; and after him Antigonus of Soko (whose disciples, we have said, were Zadok and Boethus). Antigonus took the tradition from Simeon. After Antigonus came Yose b. Yoezer and Yose b. Yoḥanan, who learned from him. After these two came Joshua b. Peraḥyah (said to have been the maternal uncle of Yeshua b. Pandera, who is Jesus son of Mary),[{6a}] together with Nittai of Arbela. After them came Judah b. Tabbai and Simeon b. Sheṭaḥ. After them came Shemaʿyah and Avṭalion. After them came Hillel and Shammai — between whom and their disciples the great split arose, with one school excommunicating the other; this split, they say, was resolved on a single day in the upper room of Ḥananyah b. Ḥizqiyah b. Garon. The school of Shammai became the Palestinian school; the school of Hillel, the Babylonian. They further claim that Hillel had eighty disciples: thirty worthy of having the Shekhinah dwell upon them as upon Moses; thirty worthy of having the sun stand still for them as for Joshua; and twenty of intermediate rank.[{6}] The greatest of these eighty was Jonathan b. Uzziel — who translated the prophetic books into Aramaic (the Targum). The smallest was Yoḥanan b. Zakkai. Yoḥanan b. Zakkai had five disciples, including Eliezer b. Hyrcanus and Eleazar b. ʿArakh. It is said that "if all the wise men of Israel were on one side of the scale and Eliezer b. Hyrcanus on the other, he would outweigh them all." This man — Eliezer — is the first named figure in the Mishnah; together with Gamaliel, who was his brother-in-law (his sister's husband). How then can the Mishnah possibly be claimed as a transmitted document, when the first named figure in it is among the last members of their own chain of transmission? The matter is plainer than the plainest. None of the Rabbanites holds that the Mishnah was transmitted as written; it was composed at the end of the Second Temple period. Anyone who claims it was transmitted in writing is either ignorant or a bluffer.

A passing oddity: they claim that Jonathan b. Uzziel was in the rank of Moses (peace upon him) — yet his Targum on the prophetic books contains many absurdities. He renders (Isa 20:2), "Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins" — but Jonathan's targum makes it "tie the sackcloth on thy loins"![{7}] He renders (Isa 5:13), "and their multitude was dried up with thirst," and Hosea 11:4, "and I extended to him food" — both with similar palpable absurdities of either word or sense. Of such things he has many; they are evident even to a child, and need no further elaboration here.

We further ask them: either the Mishnah is self-sufficient — i.e., everything that was in the naql is recorded in it — or it is not. If it is self-sufficient, what then is the Talmud? What does it establish, given that everything that was in the naql has already been recorded in the Mishnah? If it is not self-sufficient — if there were matters that remained outside it — then why did the Mishnah's compilers not record them? Why did they leave them for later compilers to put down in the Talmud? This claim — that the Mishnah and Talmud are transmitted — is nothing but trickery and contrivance (talzīq wa-talfīq), invented because they could not find a single supporting verse from Scripture. They resorted to this maneuver in order to mislead the common people.

How is anyone not embarrassed to claim that this Torah — which is in the hands of the whole nation, transmitted from East to West, attested by this immense multitude — is not the Torah brought by Moses (peace upon him), and at the same time to demand that we accept the Mishnah and Talmud, which are in the hands of a small group on whom collusion is fully possible, as a transmission from prophecy? Whoever maintains such a position has made truth into falsehood and falsehood into truth: he has allowed that the Torah, which has been transmitted by sound naql, may have been abrogated and removed, and at the same time he has set up what is not transmitted as if it were transmitted. We will continue this argument in our treatment of naql and ijmāʿ proper (Babs 14–18 below).

Finally: is there anything remaining of the farāʾiḍ and aḥkām that is not recorded in the Mishnah and Talmud — and that requires qiyās and istikhrāj — or is there nothing remaining: is everything fully covered by codification? If they say something remains, their claim that the naql exhausts the matter is refuted, and istikhrāj and qiyās are obligatory. If they say everything is covered, their position is corrupt on two grounds. First, new cases continually arise in the world that require the application of subtle rulings — cases that cannot in principle have been enumerated in advance; no prophet could have foreseen and addressed every future case of detailed law; the supposition that he did so is in the highest degree absurd. Second, we observe in their own current practice that when a person poses a question to two Reshei Yeshiva (roʾush al-mathībāt), each of them answers and rules differently from the other. Were everything fixed and codified by naql, no such disagreement could arise. So each of them is answering and ruling by extraction and qiyās. They have no escape from this; and in it lies the establishment of qiyās and the fall of what they claim about naql. ---
